newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK deals in a slow market.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK deals in a slow market.

text.p: International Bank of Asia launched its HK$1.0 billion multi-currency floating rate certificate of deposit issue into a slow Asian debt market on Thursday.
The certificates are available in either Hong Kong or U.S. dollars. Both tranches mature in three years.

The Hong Kong dollar tranche pays a margin of 50 basis points and, with fees, an all-in return of 72 basis points. The U.S. dollar tranche pays a margin of 40 basis points and an all-in return of 57 basis points.
The issue will not be eligible for use as collateral at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), or discount window.
Bankers characterized the pricing as reasonable compared with other similar credits.
Fuji International Finance (HK), Bayerisch Landesbank Hong Kong, Standard Chartered Bank, WestLB Hong Kong and Sakura Finance Asia are arrangers for the deal.
Among other issues, Wing Hang Bank's FRCD issue has been increased to HK$1.38 billion from HK$1.2 billion due to oversubscription, arranger Jardine Fleming Bank said.
A HK$6 billion loan for a property consortium involved in Hong Kong's Mass Transit Railway Corp airport railway development at the Tung Chung Station Package Two site has been launched, bankers said.

HKR International, Hong Leong Holding and Recosia Pte Ltd, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Singapore Ministry of Finance, each own 30 percent of the project. The remaining 10 percent is held by Hong Kong China Ltd.
Shareholders will offer guarantees for the loan in proportion to their equity stake in the project.
The four-year facility pays a margin of 110 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate.
Commitment fees are 12.5 basis points.

Underwriting fees are 12.5 basis points for arrangers and senior lead managers committing HK$400 million to HK$500 million and 10 basis points for arrangers and lead managers committing HK$300 million to HK$350 million.
Management fees are 57.5 basis points for both levels.
The development, with a total gross floor area of 2.04 million square feet, is estimated to cost about HK$9 billion.

Moody's Investors Service, in a statement released overnight, said that "Hong Kong's A3 foreign currency debt ceiling is appropriate given the transition to Chinese sovereignty and existing strong ties to the People's Republic."
Moody's rates Hong Kong and China equally at A3.
On Wednesday, Standard and Poor's Corp raised Hong Kong's foreign currency rating to A-plus and China's rating to BBB-plus, maintaining the three-notch gap between the two.

In other news, a senior executive at the company developing China's Three Gorges dam said he does not rule out issuing bonds overseas to supplement development capital needed to build the world's largest hydroelectric dam.

"This (overseas bond issues) must be approved by the central government, but in my personal opinion we must use foreign funds," Qin Zhongyi, vice president of China Yangtze Three Gorges Project Development Corp said on Thursday.

The Three Gorges dam has stirred some controversy because of its impact on the environment and the people living nearby. Hundreds of thousands of people residing near the dam are scheduled to be re-located to make way for the project.
